concepts.name: Check
concepts.summary: A king is in check when an enemy piece attacks it. The player in check must get out of it at once: move the king, block the check, or capture the checking piece.

concepts.name: Checkmate
concepts.summary: Checkmate is check with no way out: the king is attacked and no legal move stops the attack. Checkmate ends the game.

concepts.name: Mate in one
concepts.summary: A checkmate that takes a single move. Always look at every check first — one of them may end the game.

concepts.name: Stalemate
concepts.summary: Stalemate: the player to move is NOT in check but has no legal move. The game is a draw — a big danger when you are winning.

concepts.name: Castling
concepts.summary: Castling moves the king two squares towards a rook and puts the rook on the other side of the king, in one move. It tucks the king away and brings the rook into play.

concepts.name: When you can't castle
concepts.summary: You may not castle if the king or that rook has moved, if you are in check, if a piece stands between them, or if the king would pass through or land on an attacked square.

concepts.name: En passant
concepts.summary: En passant: when a pawn moves two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that enemy pawn may capture it as if it had moved only one square — but only on the very next move.

concepts.name: Promotion
concepts.summary: A pawn that reaches the last rank is promoted: it becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same colour — almost always a queen.

concepts.name: Captures
concepts.summary: A piece captures by moving onto a square occupied by an enemy piece, which is removed from the board. Pawns capture diagonally forward.

concepts.name: Legal and illegal moves
concepts.summary: A move is illegal if the piece can't move that way, or if it would leave your own king in check — for example moving a piece that is pinned to the king.

concepts.name: King safety
concepts.summary: Keep your king safe: castle early, keep the pawns in front of the king, and don't open lines towards it.

concepts.name: Tactics
concepts.summary: Tactics are short forcing sequences that win material or give mate: forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks and more.

concepts.name: Fork
concepts.summary: A fork is one piece attacking two or more enemy pieces at once. The opponent can usually save only one of them.

concepts.name: Knight fork
concepts.summary: Knights are the best forking pieces: they jump, and their attack can't be blocked.

concepts.name: Pawn fork
concepts.summary: A pawn attacks two squares diagonally forward. Pushed between two pieces, it attacks both — and a pawn is cheaper than anything it hits.

concepts.name: Queen fork
concepts.summary: The queen moves in eight directions, so it can often attack two loose pieces — or the king and a piece — at once.

concepts.name: Double attack
concepts.summary: A double attack is one move that creates two threats at once — by one piece (a fork) or by two pieces.

concepts.name: Pin
concepts.summary: A pin: a bishop, rook or queen attacks a piece that can't move away without exposing something more valuable behind it.

concepts.name: Absolute pin
concepts.summary: In an absolute pin the piece behind is the king, so the pinned piece may not legally move at all.

concepts.name: Relative pin
concepts.summary: In a relative pin the piece behind is valuable (not the king): the pinned piece may move, but it would lose material.

concepts.name: Skewer
concepts.summary: A skewer is a pin in reverse: a line piece attacks a valuable piece, and when it moves away, the piece behind it is captured.

concepts.name: Discovered attack
concepts.summary: A discovered attack: one piece moves out of the way and uncovers an attack by the piece behind it — two threats with one move.

concepts.name: Discovered check
concepts.summary: A discovered check: moving one piece reveals check from another. The piece that moved is free to grab something while the king deals with the check.

concepts.name: Double check
concepts.summary: Double check: two pieces give check at once. Blocking or capturing can't stop both, so the king must move.

concepts.name: Deflection
concepts.summary: Deflection lures a defender away from its job — then the square or piece it guarded falls.

concepts.name: Overloaded piece
concepts.summary: An overloaded piece has two defensive jobs at once. Attack one of them and the other collapses.

concepts.name: Removing the defender
concepts.summary: Capture (or chase away) the piece that defends something, and what it defended is left hanging.

concepts.name: Zwischenzug (in-between move)
concepts.summary: A zwischenzug is an in-between move: instead of the expected recapture, you first play a stronger forcing move.

concepts.name: Trapped piece
concepts.summary: A trapped piece is attacked and has no safe square to go to, so it will be lost.

concepts.name: Free pieces (hanging pieces)
concepts.summary: A hanging piece is one that is attacked and not defended. Always check: can I take something for free?

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.summary: A sacrifice gives up material on purpose to get something bigger: a mating attack, or even more material back.

concepts.name: Back-rank mate
concepts.summary: A back-rank mate: a rook or queen mates the king on its first rank, where its own pawns stop it from escaping.

concepts.name: Smothered mate
concepts.summary: A smothered mate: a knight mates a king that is completely surrounded by its own pieces.

concepts.name: Anastasia's mate
concepts.summary: Anastasia's mate: a knight and a rook (or queen) trap the king on the edge of the board, next to its own pawn.

concepts.name: Arabian mate
concepts.summary: The Arabian mate: a rook next to the king, protected by a knight that also covers the king's escape square.

concepts.name: Boden's mate
concepts.summary: Boden's mate: two bishops on crossing diagonals mate a king (often after queenside castling).

concepts.name: Ladder mate
concepts.summary: The ladder (lawnmower) mate: two rooks or queens take turns checking and push the king rank by rank to the edge.

concepts.name: Scholar's mate
concepts.summary: Scholar's mate: the queen, backed by the bishop, takes on f7 (or f2) with checkmate in the first few moves.

concepts.name: Fool's mate
concepts.summary: Fool's mate is the fastest possible checkmate: after two weakening pawn moves, the queen mates on move two.

concepts.name: Légal's mate
concepts.summary: Légal's mate: a queen 'sacrifice' that isn't — if the opponent grabs the queen, three minor pieces mate the king.

concepts.name: Endgames
concepts.summary: The endgame: few pieces are left, the king becomes a fighting piece, and pawns race to promote.

concepts.name: Endgames with given material
concepts.summary: Practical endgame positions with an exact material balance for each side (for example two rooks against a queen), generated and verified on request.

concepts.name: King and queen mate
concepts.summary: King and queen against a lone king always wins: the queen boxes the king in, your king comes closer, and together they mate on the edge. Beware of stalemate!

concepts.name: King and rook mate
concepts.summary: King and rook against a lone king always wins: the rook cuts the king off, your king takes the opposition, and the rook mates on the edge.

concepts.name: Opposition
concepts.summary: Kings are in opposition when they face each other with one square between them. The side NOT to move has the opposition — and in pawn endings that often decides the game.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.summary: A passed pawn has no enemy pawns in front of it or on the neighbouring files. Nothing but pieces can stop it from promoting.

concepts.name: Lucena position
concepts.summary: The Lucena position is the key winning rook endgame: king in front of its pawn on the 7th rank. White wins by 'building a bridge' with the rook.

concepts.name: Openings
concepts.summary: The opening is the first phase of the game: develop your pieces, fight for the centre, and get your king safe.

concepts.name: Italian Game
concepts.summary: The Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4): White develops quickly and aims the bishop at f7, Black's weakest point.

concepts.name: Two Knights Defense
concepts.summary: In the Two Knights Defense (3...Nf6) Black counterattacks e4 instead of copying White's bishop move — sharp and tactical.

concepts.name: Fried Liver Attack
concepts.summary: The Fried Liver Attack: White sacrifices a knight on f7 to drag Black's king into the open.

names: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Fried Liver Attack

concepts.name: Evans Gambit
concepts.summary: The Evans Gambit (4.b4): White gives a pawn to gain time for a big centre and fast development.

concepts.name: Caro-Kann Defense
concepts.summary: The Caro-Kann (1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5): a solid defence where Black challenges the centre and usually develops the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6.

concepts.name: Beginner mistakes
concepts.summary: The most common ways games are lost early: loose pieces, ignored threats, an early queen, slow development and an unsafe king.

concepts.name: Hanging a piece
concepts.summary: Hanging a piece means leaving it attacked and undefended, so the opponent simply takes it. Before every move ask: what does my move leave unprotected?

concepts.name: Hanging the queen
concepts.summary: The costliest blunder: putting the queen where it can be taken. Check every square your queen goes to for attackers.

concepts.name: Missing a threat
concepts.summary: Before you play your idea, ask what your opponent's last move threatens. Ignoring a threat is how most games are lost.

concepts.name: Spotting threats
concepts.summary: Before you move, ask what your opponent is threatening. If a piece of yours can be taken for free, deal with that first: move it, defend it, or block the attack.

concepts.name: Walking into a fork
concepts.summary: Walking into a fork: a move puts two pieces (or king and piece) where one enemy piece can attack both.

concepts.name: Grabbing poisoned material
concepts.summary: Poisoned material: a pawn or piece that looks free, but taking it costs more than it gains.

concepts.name: Weakening the king
concepts.summary: Moving the pawns in front of your king, or walking the king into the open, lets enemy pieces reach it.
aliases: pushing pawns in front of the king

concepts.name: Bringing the queen out early
concepts.summary: Bringing the queen out early lets the opponent develop with tempo — every new piece attacks your queen.

concepts.name: Moving the same piece repeatedly
concepts.summary: Moving one piece again and again in the opening wastes time: the opponent develops while you shuffle.

concepts.name: Ignoring development
concepts.summary: Pawn moves and queen trips don't develop pieces. Fall behind in development and the opponent attacks with more pieces.

concepts.name: Decoy
concepts.summary: A decoy gives up material to drag an enemy piece — often the king — onto a square where it can be hit: the capture walks straight into a check, a fork or a mate.

concepts.name: Clearance
concepts.summary: A clearance move gets one of your own pieces out of the way — ideally with a threat — so another piece can use the square or line it was blocking.

concepts.name: Interference
concepts.summary: Interference puts a piece between an enemy long-range piece and a square it guards. With the line cut, that square is no longer defended.

concepts.name: Underpromotion
concepts.summary: Promoting to a knight, bishop or rook instead of a queen. It is rare, but sometimes a knight gives a winning check, or a queen would stalemate.

concepts.name: Mate in two
concepts.summary: A forced checkmate in two moves: the first move — often a check or a sacrifice — leaves no defence against the mate that follows.

concepts.name: Hook mate
concepts.summary: A hook mate: a rook mates from right next to the king, guarded by a knight that is itself guarded by a pawn.

concepts.name: Dovetail mate
concepts.summary: A dovetail mate: the queen mates from a square diagonally next to the king, and the king's own pieces block the two escape squares she doesn't cover.

concepts.name: Rule of the square
concepts.summary: Draw a square from the pawn to its promotion square. If the defending king can't step into that square, it can never catch the pawn — just push it.
aliases: can the king catch the pawn

concepts.name: Key squares
concepts.summary: In king and pawn against king, the attacking king wins if it reaches a key square — usually two squares in front of the pawn. Then the pawn walks in.

concepts.name: Philidor position
concepts.summary: The basic rook-ending draw: keep your rook on your third rank so the enemy king can't come forward. When the pawn steps onto that rank, drop the rook back and check from behind.

concepts.name: Triangulation
concepts.summary: Triangulation: the king takes three moves to come back to a square it could reach in two, so the same position returns with the opponent to move.

concepts.name: Wrong bishop
concepts.summary: Bishop and rook pawn can't win if the bishop doesn't control the promotion square: the defending king sits in the corner and it is a draw.

concepts.name: Outside passed pawn
concepts.summary: A passed pawn far from the other pawns: the enemy king has to run over to stop it, and your king walks in and eats the pawns on the other side.

concepts.name: Pawn breakthrough
concepts.summary: In a pawn ending, giving up one or two pawns to break the enemy pawn chain so that one of your pawns runs through to promote.

concepts.name: Ignoring the back rank
concepts.summary: With no escape square for the king, a single rook or queen check on the back rank can be mate. Before you move a defender away, check your back rank.

concepts.name: Avoiding stalemate
concepts.summary: When you are winning, check that your opponent still has a legal move. No legal move and no check is stalemate — a draw thrown away.

concepts.name: X-ray
concepts.summary: An x-ray attacks through an enemy piece: a rook, bishop or queen stands behind that piece on the same line, and as soon as the piece in between moves or is exchanged, the long-range piece strikes on the square behind it.

concepts.name: Double-bishop mate
concepts.summary: A double-bishop mate: one bishop gives check while the other bishop, on the other colour, takes away the king's escape squares.

concepts.name: Epaulette mate
concepts.summary: In an epaulette mate the king is boxed in on both sides by its own pieces (often rooks), like shoulder pads, and a queen gives check from directly in front of it.

concepts.name: Greek gift sacrifice
concepts.summary: The Greek gift is a bishop sacrifice on h7 (or h2) against a castled king, usually followed by a knight check on g5 (g4) and the queen joining the attack. It only works when those follow-up moves really are available, so check the defender's replies before sacrificing.

concepts.name: Windmill
concepts.summary: A windmill is a repeated discovered check: one piece moves back and forth, uncovering check from a rook or bishop behind it each time, and uses every move to capture something.

concepts.name: Desperado
concepts.summary: A desperado is a piece that is lost anyway: before it is taken, it captures something, so at least it is sold for material instead of given away for nothing.

concepts.name: Zugzwang
concepts.summary: Zugzwang is a position where the side to move would be fine if it could pass, but every legal move makes its position worse. A quiet move that hands the opponent the move can decide the game.

concepts.name: Perpetual check
concepts.summary: Perpetual check is a series of checks the opponent can't escape. It saves a lost game: the same position repeats and the game is drawn.

concepts.name: Stalemate tricks
concepts.summary: A stalemate trick saves a lost game: the losing side gets rid of its last moves so that it is left with no legal move while not in check — and stalemate is a draw.
